content: Postoperative pain is a significant issue in pediatric surgery, and premedication with an appropriate agent may help manage this pain more effectively. Clonidine, an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, possesses sedative, anxiolytic, and analgesic properties, making it a potential candidate for premedication to reduce postoperative pain in children. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of clonidine as a premedication in reducing postoperative pain in children under 18 years of age. Additionally, the study aimed to identify any clinically significant side effects associated with its use. A comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, and Ovid EMBASE, up to December 21, 2012. Reference lists of relevant articles and online trial registries were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria encompassed randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing clonidine premedication to placebo, higher doses of clonidine, or other agents in children undergoing surgery or invasive procedures, with pain or surrogate outcomes (e.g., need for additional analgesia) reported. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Data were analyzed using RevMan 5, and sensitivity analyses were performed to exclude studies with a high risk of bias. A total of 11 trials involving 742 children were included. The risk of bias in these studies was generally low or unclear, although two studies had methodological aspects with a high risk of bias. The overall quality of evidence from the pooled studies was low or unclear. The trials exhibited substantial methodological heterogeneity, including variations in clonidine dosage, administration routes, patient populations, surgical procedures, and outcome measures, which complicated meta-analysis. Four trials compared clonidine to placebo or no treatment. When clonidine was administered orally at a dose of 4 µg/kg, the need for additional analgesia was significantly reduced (risk ratio [RR] 0.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.11 to 0.51). One small trial (15 patients per group) compared oral clonidine (2 or 4 µg/kg) to oral midazolam (0.5 mg/kg) and found a similar reduction in the need for additional postoperative analgesia (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.71). A trial comparing oral clonidine (4 µg/kg) to intravenous fentanyl (3 µg/kg) found no statistically significant difference in the need for rescue analgesia (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.42). When comparing clonidine at 4 µg/kg to 2 µg/kg, a single high-quality trial reported a significant reduction in the number of patients requiring additional analgesia with the higher dose (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.65). However, interpreting the effect of clonidine on pain scores was challenging due to differences in study methodologies, drug dosages, administration routes, and pain scales used. Nonetheless, clonidine at 4 µg/kg appeared to reduce the need for postoperative analgesia. No significant adverse effects, such as severe hypotension, bradycardia, or excessive sedation requiring intervention, were reported. However, several studies used prophylactic atropine to prevent such side effects. In conclusion, only 11 trials involving 742 children were identified, and despite heterogeneity among the studies, clonidine premedication at an adequate dose (4 µg/kg) likely provides a beneficial effect on postoperative pain in children. Side effects were minimal, although some studies used atropine prophylactically to mitigate potential adverse effects. Further research is needed to determine the optimal conditions under which clonidine premedication is most effective for postoperative pain relief in pediatric patients.
